whyItMatters: Every Java program, from a ten-line exercise to a banking system, is built from the same few structural pieces: classes, methods, statements and blocks. When you can read that structure at a glance, compiler errors stop looking like noise and start pointing at specific lines. Syntax is also the vocabulary every later topic assumes.
mentalModel:
Think of a Java file as nested boxes. A class is the outer box. Methods are boxes inside it. Statements are the individual instructions inside a method, each closed with a semicolon. Curly braces mark where a box opens and closes, so every `{` needs a matching `}`.

The JVM does not run the whole file at once. It starts at exactly one place, the `main` method, and runs its statements from top to bottom.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting the semicolon at the end of a statement.
commonMistakes.fix: The compiler reports `';' expected`, often on the line after the real mistake. End every statement with `;`.

commonMistakes.mistake: Naming the file differently from the public class.
commonMistakes.fix: `public class Greeter` must be in `Greeter.java`, with identical capitalization.
Java is case-sensitive. The class is `System`; the compiler says `package system does not exist`.
`reached end of file while parsing` means a `{` was never closed. Indent consistently so mismatches are easy to see.

commonMistakes.mistake: Changing the `main` signature, for example `public static void main()`.
commonMistakes.fix: Without a `String[]` parameter the launcher cannot use it as the entry point. Keep the exact signature.

comparisons.summary: Syntax rules are checked by `javac` before anything runs. The program lifecycle explains what happens after your syntax is accepted: loading, verification and execution by the JVM.

notes.text: Declares a class named `Greeter`. Because it is `public`, the file must be named `Greeter.java`.
A comment. The compiler ignores everything from `//` to the end of the line.
The entry point. `public` lets the JVM call it, `static` means no object is needed first, `void` means it returns nothing, and `String[] args` receives command-line arguments.
Two variable declarations: a type, a name, `=`, a value, and a closing semicolon.
`System.out.println(...)` prints one line. The `+` joins text and other values into a single string.
Closing braces. The first ends `main`, the second ends the class; each matches an opening brace.
